summary: Describes the high-level requirements for exchanging intrusion detection information, including data formats and exchange procedures, as set out by the Intrusion Detection Exchange Format Working Group.

eli5.summary: Before building a way for alarm systems to share reports, the working group wrote down what that sharing would need to do. This is that wish list.

questions: what must an intrusion detection exchange protocol do
what is intrusion detection message exchange format
how should ids systems share alerts
subtitle: Specification requirements for exchanging intrusion detection alerts between systems.

tldr.problem: Different intrusion detection systems produce alerts in different formats, making it difficult to correlate attacks across multiple systems or organizations, or to integrate components from different vendors.
tldr.mechanism: The Intrusion Detection Exchange Format Working Group (IDWG) defined a set of high-level requirements for both the format of alert messages and the protocol used to communicate them, enabling interoperability.
tldr.outcome: These requirements drove the creation of the IDMEF (Intrusion Detection Message Exchange Format) standard, allowing heterogeneous IDS systems to share detection data in a common format.

facts.label: Alert types
facts.value: Detected events from network, host, or application sources

today: RFC 4766 is an Informational RFC describing the requirements that led to the development of the IDMEF specification. While the RFC itself is stable, the IDMEF format has continued to evolve, and organizations implementing IDS alert sharing now have multiple protocol options including IDMEF and syslog-based approaches for communicating security events.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 4766 describes the requirements that drove the design of the Intrusion Detection Message Exchange Format (IDMEF), a standard format for reporting security events detected by intrusion detection systems. The document defines requirements for both the message format itself and the communication protocol that carries those messages between IDS components.

The RFC was produced by the Intrusion Detection Exchange Format Working Group (IDWG) to address a practical problem: organizations deploy multiple intrusion detection systems from different vendors because each product has different strengths and weaknesses, but no standard exists for these systems to report findings to each other or to a central management console in a machine-readable format. This fragmentation makes threat correlation and incident response inefficient.
sections.eli5: When you have security cameras from different makers in your house, you want them all to send alerts to the same app. This document lists what all those alerts need to contain.

sections.title: Architectural Model and Terminology
sections.content:
The RFC defines a clear model of IDS components. A sensor collects raw data from the network, file system, or application logs. An analyzer examines that data for signs of unauthorized activity and generates alerts when it detects something interesting. A manager receives and presents alerts to human operators, who decide what response actions to take (logging, blocking, terminating sessions, etc.). An event is the raw occurrence in the data source; an activity is the interpretation of that event as suspicious.

The requirements assume that an analyzer and a manager are separate components communicating over TCP/IP, though implementations may combine or distribute these components differently. The document avoids prescribing architectural details like whether the sensor and analyzer are integrated, or whether a component might simultaneously act as a manager for some connections and an analyzer for others.
sections.eli5: A sensor watches what is happening. An analyzer thinks about whether it is suspicious. A manager collects reports and decides what to do. Each can talk to the others.

sections.title: Message Format and Content
sections.content:
The document requires that IDMEF messages support internationalization and localization, allowing alerts to be presented to operators in their local language and format. Messages must support filtering and aggregation, so operators can suppress low-priority events or combine related alerts into summaries, reducing noise.

Content requirements specify that messages must convey the detected data (what triggered the alert), event identity (a unique identifier for the event), source and target addresses (supporting both IPv4 and IPv6), impact assessment (severity, whether the attack succeeded), analyzer location and identity, a confidence level in the detection, and proper timestamp information with synchronized time across systems. Timestamps must be granular enough to correlate related events and in a standardized format.
sections.eli5: Alerts need to say what happened, who did it, who it happened to, how serious it was, when it happened, which alarm system found it, and how sure that system is.

sections.title: Communication Protocol Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC specifies that the communication protocol (called IDMEF Communication Protocol or IDP) must provide reliable message transmission, ensuring alerts are not lost. It must work with firewalls, not requiring administrative access to firewall rules. The protocol must support mutual authentication of analyzer and manager, message confidentiality to prevent eavesdropping, and message integrity to detect tampering.

Additional requirements include per-source authentication (knowing which analyzer sent a particular alert), denial-of-service resistance (not crashing when flooded with alerts or false messages), and duplicate detection (identifying when the same alert is sent multiple times). The document notes that these requirements can be met by existing IETF protocols and does not mandate that a new protocol be created.
sections.eli5: Alerts must not get lost, must not be read by snoops, must not be changed in transit, must say who sent them, and must not crash the system.

sections.title: Design Principles and Extensibility
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that the IDMEF message format should be independent of the transport protocol, allowing the same format to be used over HTTP, SNMP, or other protocols without change. This enforces a clean separation between the semantics of what an alert contains and the mechanics of how it is delivered.

Messages must support extensions for vendor-specific information or future capabilities, but extensions must be designed carefully to avoid breaking compatibility with implementations that do not recognize them. The RFC warns that overreliance on proprietary extensions harms interoperability.
sections.eli5: The message format should not care how it is sent. New types of information can be added to alerts, but done carefully so old systems do not break.
